78YGmvETrOA.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: The Rituals, Episode 15
78YGmvETrOA.one_line: Reviewing the rules of tazkiyah, then opening the salah series: why prayer lost its life, and two first tips on wudu and a pause before prayer.
78YGmvETrOA.summary: He reviews the framework: everyone, even an atheist, has a creed, a way of worship and an ethic, and only you can hold yourself to your morals. He restates the four rules, adding that he leaves topics open on purpose because spoon-feeding kills curiosity, and that resistance to exercises is the nafs, not reason. After the daily focuses, especially that every deed remains pending, he turns to salah, the ritual that will take most of the series. A lifetime holds only about 150,000 obligatory prayers, they are the first thing judged, and they are the relationship with Allah from which every other deed draws its sincerity. Salah was once spiritual fuel but has become an empty, autopilot movement that Muslims experience as a burden. The coming tips are temporary fixes while deeper tazkiyah works. Tip one: perform wudu with presence, as outer cleansing that reflects an inner pursuit of purity. Tip two, the most important and least followed: pause ten seconds before the opening takbir, set aside what you were thinking, write down pressing thoughts or bring them to Allah as a conversation. Change must be gradual and consistent, a battle of wills with the nafs like raising a child.

outline.heading: Everyone has a creed, a way of worship and an ethic
outline.gist: Even atheism is a way of understanding the world; the question is whether you choose these three deliberately and properly. In Islam spirituality means holding yourself to an honest ethical standard.

outline.gist: Law cannot judge intentions. Tazkiyah's comprehension work defines intangible concepts like humility, and ideas end up defining who you are.

outline.heading: Why perfect the rituals
outline.gist: A ritual that benefits neither you nor society and is not accepted is empty; the series starts with salah.

outline.heading: Rule: everything is about you
outline.gist: Never use what you learn to impress or belittle others; until you understand it deeply, apply it only to yourself.

outline.heading: Rule: commit to the daily wird
outline.gist: Committing to dhikr you are not obliged to do builds character; three adhkar a hundred times each, twice a day.

outline.heading: Rule: contemplation, and why topics are left open
outline.gist: He deliberately leaves topics incomplete; being spoon-fed kills curiosity, as modern education shows compared with those who discovered equations by struggling.

outline.heading: A method of thinking, not answers
outline.gist: His role is to give a way of reasoning so you can solve your own ethical struggles; contemplation is what raised the Prophet.

outline.heading: Rule: exercises, and telling yourself from your nafs
outline.gist: Refusing an exercise is the nafs, not reason; learning to tell the rational self from the nafs is how you discover your real intentions.

outline.heading: Daily focuses: the second layer, servanthood and intention
outline.gist: Every act has a why behind the what; ask whether you behave as a true servant, and never stop trying to improve intentions even slightly.

outline.heading: Daily focus: every deed is pending
outline.gist: No deed is known to be accepted; showing Allah satisfaction with oneself could be a reason for rejection, so keep pushing.

outline.heading: Salah as the foundation of all other deeds
outline.gist: About 150,000 obligatory prayers in a life; they are judged first and show whether your deeds were for Allah, as salah is the connection with Him.

outline.heading: Salah as fuel, not a burden
outline.gist: Allah gains nothing from it; earlier Muslims felt it as strength, and night prayer prepared the Prophet to carry a heavy word.

outline.heading: Tips as band-aids for deeper work
outline.gist: Real improvement needs work on self-value, humility and mortality, but small fixes can lift salah in the meantime.

outline.heading: Tip one: wudu as outer purity reflecting inner purity
outline.gist: Rituals put the body in a state meant to be mirrored spiritually, as the two plain sheets of ihram reflect humility and equality.

outline.heading: How salah lost its life
outline.gist: Jibril taught wudu and salah first; it built a nation that speaks to Allah daily. Outsiders see us as deeply spiritual while we feel nothing, because only the movement remains.

outline.heading: Making wudu with presence
outline.gist: Do not make wudu while watching videos or on the phone; pause for a moment to remember you are preparing to stand before the King of kings.

outline.heading: Interlude
Sins falling with the water of wudu
outline.gist: The narration of sins leaving with the drops, and Abu Hanifa's early view that used wudu water was impure, said to come from seeing the sins in it.

outline.heading: Tip two: pause briefly before the takbir
outline.gist: Before raising your hands, stop and remember where you are and whom you are addressing; salah must be a time-out, not a continuation of your thoughts.

outline.heading: Writing down thoughts before prayer
outline.gist: He keeps a salah note on his phone to park pressing thoughts; for the Prophet salah was a refuge from people's needs, unlike our autopilot prayer.

outline.heading: Finish the thought, or bring it to Allah
outline.gist: If a thought will not stop, finish it first or carry it into salah as a request to Allah; nothing is too small to discuss with Him, and the takbir symbolises putting things behind you.

outline.heading: Focus on the obligatory prayers prayed alone
outline.gist: The fard prayers are what you will be asked about; praying in jamaah is easier because the imam carries much of it.

outline.heading: Why salah feels like a burden
outline.gist: If life continues into salah it becomes a hindrance; we already pause our problems to meet friends, and the nafs resists only because it sees no value in prayer.

outline.heading: Gradual change and consistency
outline.gist: Practise two tips a week; trying everything at once will fail, because the nafs breaks under radical change and must be bent slowly.

outline.heading: Outlasting the will of the inner child
outline.gist: Raising a child is a battle of wills, and the nafs is the same five-year-old inside; you win by outlasting it, not by losing your temper.

outline.heading: Outro

q3eHMwANMYw.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Panic, Impatience and Stinginess
q3eHMwANMYw.one_line: Al-Ma'arij 19-21: man is created panicky, impatient in hardship, withholding in ease; salah must turn that into perseverance and generosity, eman's two halves.
q3eHMwANMYw.summary: He prefaces the series with Truth and Reconciliation Day. He distrusts token days, but the point for Muslims is that the murder, enslavement and residential schools inflicted on this land's Indigenous peoples must count as oppression equal to anything done to Muslims in China, India, Somalia, Sudan or Palestine; righteousness cannot be cherry-picked or the cause stops being godly. Muslims stand with the oppressed regardless of religion or race, hold back a brother who oppresses, and walk this land humbly as guests whose hosts were never asked. Then the week's verses: man was created halu', panicky, a survival trait that now needs taming. When difficulty touches him he is jazu', impatient, needing it to end now; when good touches him he is manu', withholding what he could give. A three-year-old shows both reflexes, and adults only mask them. The exception is those who pray, whose prayer and book retrain them into perseverance and generosity. Manu' appears once more, in Al-Ma'un, describing worshippers who still withhold: a salah that leaves you stingy and panicky has missed its point. Perseverance is half of eman and gratitude, expressed as giving, the other half. Ayyub was ashamed to ask for relief, the Prophet gave like one who fears no poverty, and the companions carried illness and loss with a grace that fooled everyone.

outline.heading: Opening
Truth and Reconciliation Day: what was done to this land
outline.gist: He has never liked the days offered to persecuted peoples so they can be remembered for a moment and forgotten. Europeans, called settlers to avoid saying colonialists, took this land by murder and enslavement, then ran over a hundred residential schools that tore children from their parents to erase their identity and language, only decades ago.

outline.heading: Equal care for every oppressed people
outline.gist: A day a year will not make up for it, and the oppression has never been removed. The point for Muslims: unless you see it as equal in atrocity to what is done to Muslims in China, India, Somalia, Sudan or anywhere else, we will not solve our own problems.

outline.heading: You cannot cherry-pick oppression
outline.gist: Righteousness is one thing: either you recognize all oppression as oppression or you do not. Once you treat the suffering of people who look like you as more important, your cause stops being godly, loses its moral standing and eventually fails.

outline.heading: Justice regardless of religion or race
outline.gist: The people of truth and the people of oppression can be Muslim or not; on justice Muslims look at neither deen, colour, culture nor race. The day reminds us that what happened here is what is happening in Palestine and has happened to many peoples, and this is the one ethic never compromised.

outline.heading: Hold back your brother who oppresses
outline.gist: The Prophet said to support your brother whether oppressor or oppressed; asked how to support an oppressor, he said hold him back. If he is on your side and oppressing, you cannot stay neutral because he is a Muslim brother.

outline.heading: A wrong that will never be fixed in this world
outline.gist: Recognize the land we stand on and the descendants of its owners, who will never get it back. Some rights will never return to their owners in this life, so we walk this land with humility, humbleness and respect.

outline.heading: Guests on this land
outline.gist: We are guests of people who never got to choose whether they wanted guests, and acknowledging that is part of acknowledging the rights of the people of Palestine and elsewhere. The Quran's first interest was to change character, telling people how they behave and what must stop.

outline.heading: Last week's pairs, and today's intrinsic trait
outline.gist: The companions who applied this changed the world. Last week: when you get what you want, gratitude instead of entitlement; when you get what you fear, resilience instead of despair; when you ask, contentment instead of greed. Today is a trait more intrinsic than wanting or fearing.

outline.heading: Created halu': quick to lose composure
outline.gist: Al-Ma'arij 70:19: the human being was created halu', a part of everyone's nature that cannot be escaped, only managed. The best English is panicky: quick to panic and lose composure.

outline.heading: A survival trait that outlived the jungle
outline.gist: It is rooted in a deep fear: we were designed to survive, and in the wilderness whoever is calm and quick to trust is taken out early. We no longer live in the jungle, but the quality stays with us.

outline.heading: Why 'evil' touches him
outline.gist: The Quran rarely calls hardship evil, because difficulty met with perseverance is rewarded. It says evil in 70:20 because that is how the human sees it; in reality there is only ease and difficulty, turned good by perseverance and gratitude or evil by losing composure, as squandered wealth can be.

outline.heading: Jazu': it has to end now
outline.gist: Touched by difficulty, he is jazu', the opposite of perseverance: impatient and needing whatever has come his way to end quickly. Ayyub lost his health, wealth and family, and even his standing, since no one listened to him.

outline.heading: Ayyub, ashamed to ask for relief
outline.gist: He lost everything an accomplished man could lose and stayed patient. When his wife asked why he would not pray for relief, he said he was ashamed to ask before spending as long in difficulty as he had in ease, sixty years, as the books of tafsir report.

outline.heading: Manu': withholding what you could give
outline.gist: Impatience is saying "I can't take it anymore, enough is enough". Al-Ma'arij 70:21: touched by ease he is manu', which has no English equivalent; stinginess is closest: holding back what you could give. This is everyone's nature, the speaker's first.

outline.heading: The three-year-old in all of us
outline.gist: The first reflex in difficulty is impatience and in ease to hold it back. A three-year-old cannot wait and will not share, not even with his mother; adults never lose the reflex, they only learn to mask it. Allah is describing, not chastising.

outline.heading: Except those who pray
outline.gist: Then come the exceptions, those who pray, and the long description of how salah and the book change them. The focus is on the verses before: the point is to stop being impatient and stingy.

outline.heading: Perseverant and generous instead
outline.gist: Embraced properly, these practices replace impatience with perseverance, so life hits hard without breaking your composure, and withholding with generosity: the more Allah gives you, the more you give. The word manu' appears only twice in the Quran, as if by design.

outline.heading: Woe to those who pray
outline.gist: The second use is in Al-Ma'un: woe to the worshippers, unusually a warning to people who pray. They were heedless of their prayer, and they withheld aid; they never changed the trait.

outline.heading: A prayer that leaves you withholding
outline.gist: Their salah did not make them generous. If you pray yet panic, sell out, compromise, steal or beg when life deals a bad hand, and hold back when you could give, what is the point of the prayer?

outline.heading: The two halves of eman
outline.gist: You cannot carry the deen like this; teach yourself and your children. Perseverance is half of eman, and the scholars made gratitude the other half: in difficulty you persevere instead of losing composure, and in ease you are grateful.

outline.heading: Gratitude shown by giving
outline.gist: Gratitude is shown by giving. Either you get what you dislike or what you like, and the first instinct is to panic or to hoard. The Prophet was described as more generous than the wind sent with rain, a big deal in the desert.

outline.heading: Interlude
The shame is not changing
outline.gist: In the Makkan period the Quran focused on changing character. Everyone here is halu', so no one is shamed for it; the shame is knowing you can change and not doing so. How to change does not fit in a khutbah: go and learn what the Quran taught.

outline.heading: He gives like one who fears no poverty
outline.gist: A man the Prophet gave great wealth went about telling people to accept whatever he teaches, because he gives as if he has no fear of poverty, though the man had hated him. Fear of being poor is the panic inside us that makes us hold back and grow impatient.

outline.heading: The four caliphs: giving and composure
outline.gist: Learn from him and from how Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali lived: they gave when they had and lived with nothing, and carried illness, death, loss and sorrow with such composure that you would think everything was fine.

outline.heading: Outro

E_TKsqn5zhc.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Muddaththir, Part 2: Verses 7-14
E_TKsqn5zhc.one_line: The seven opening commands as Islam's complete outward code, accountability as the keystone, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Mecca's godfather.
E_TKsqn5zhc.summary: He returns to the seven opening commands of Al-Muddaththir, which, unlike Al-Muzzammil's inward practices, define how a Muslim carries Islam outward: take a stand for reform, warn, live by Allah's priorities, be presentable, shun every behaviour people universally know is low, give without strings, and persevere for Allah. Praising Islam without living it is pointless, and favours done for Allah cannot later be cashed in for votes or connections. These verses came before any details of law, which differed between prophets, and they were the buy-in. During the pause in revelation the companions lived them, which is why Quraysh could spot the secret Muslims and why Islam reached even London, Ontario. He asks listeners to live by the seven commands for a week. Verses 8-10 turn to the trumpet, because no ethic holds without accountability: Hatim al-Ta'i's famous generosity rested only on reputation. The Day is hard for everyone and not easy for the disbelievers. Verse 11 tells the Prophet to leave the arrogant to Allah, which calms the rage felt when criminals are honoured. Verses 12-14 describe al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, Mecca's godfather, whose protection Uthman ibn Maz'un renounced, and whose missed opportunity sets up next week.

outline.heading: Opening
Inward commands of Al-Muzzammil, outward commands of Al-Muddaththir
outline.gist: Al-Muzzammil's eight commands are private, between you and Allah at night. The seven at the opening of Al-Muddaththir are the first commands Muslims carry into the world: what makes a Muslim stand out.

outline.heading: First: take a stand for reform
outline.gist: Rules without an overarching stand become mechanical. Qum is not standing up but taking a stand against the status quo; each prophet reformed a different corruption: Lut sexual ethics, Shu'ayb finance, Musa politics.

outline.heading: Second: warn
outline.gist: Spread the message, starting with the warning, since news of potential harm comes before news of benefit.

outline.heading: Third: magnify your Lord and live the message
outline.gist: Live by Allah's priorities. Spreading a message you do not follow defeats the purpose, and admiring Islam while breaking its every law is not cute.

outline.heading: Fourth: purify your clothing
outline.gist: Representing the message includes appearance: even your clothing must reflect it.

outline.heading: Fifth: shun the low; everyone knows what rujz is
outline.gist: Riba, gambling and alcohol are low in every society. Even an atheist politician knows not to be seen outside a strip club; cleanse your clothes of physical filth and yourself of moral filth.

outline.heading: Sixth: give without seeking more
outline.gist: A relationship command: give selflessly, never expecting praise, loyalty or support in return.

outline.heading: Seventh: persevere for your Lord
outline.gist: All of this takes perseverance, for Allah alone, since no one else deserves it.

outline.heading: Interlude
A complete way of life before any details of law
outline.gist: The seven cover intentions, ethics, appearance, way of life and purpose. The details of shari'ah came later and always differed between prophets, so they were not taught first.

outline.heading: The low is known without education
outline.gist: Carrying Islam outward means taking a stand, spreading and living the message, and being presentable. Ask an unbelieving parent whether they want it for their child, or a smoker whether he would hand a cigarette to a six-year-old.

outline.heading: Giving cannot be transactional
outline.gist: Give and walk away, or state the price upfront; do not give for Allah and later cash in for votes or connections. Those who did someone a favour made a point of never asking him for one.

outline.heading: Perseverance, and the full package
outline.gist: These commands do not happen on their own. The what, how and why of a Muslim's life are all answered in two lines.

outline.heading: Hear them as the first converts did
outline.gist: It makes you wonder what was left for 23 years of revelation. Listen as a new Muslim who knew only these early surahs and woke up knowing his purpose, stance and conduct.

outline.heading: Why Quraysh could spot the secret Muslims
outline.gist: Though the call was secret for three years, converts were obvious because their behaviour changed, and later people came to Medina to see what the fuss was about.

outline.heading: The first five surahs were the buy-in
outline.gist: If you did not like the first five surahs you were out. We memorise these verses as children but do not live by them.

outline.heading: Live by these verses for a week
outline.gist: Hold yourself to the seven commands every day: are your stance, message, priorities, appearance, conduct and purpose clear?

outline.heading: The pause in revelation: time to absorb
outline.gist: For a time this was much of the Quran. Revelation paused for around six months, grieving the Prophet until he was told he had not been forsaken; the companions used it to study and decide.

outline.heading: No introduction: orders for soldiers
outline.gist: The surah has no introduction, only a call and commands in succession, like orders handed to a soldier after Al-Muzzammil built the inner fuel.

outline.heading: From Arabia to London, Ontario
outline.gist: The Prophet's reach stayed within Arabia; the companions went beyond. A police officer in Austin did not believe London, Canada existed, yet Islam reached it, with seven or eight masjids.

outline.heading: The other early surahs carry no outward commands
outline.gist: Al-Muzzammil's commands are inward; Al-Alaq's 'read' is a principle that Islam rests on knowledge and critical thinking; Al-Fatihah has a dua. These were the soldiers' first orders.

outline.heading: Recitation of the next verses
outline.gist: He recites the verses on the trumpet that follow the commands.

outline.heading: Remove the Day and it all falls like Jenga
outline.gist: Every surah longer than half a page mentions accountability, because without it no command persuades anyone; if death is the end, nothing matters.

outline.heading: Law and reputation cannot replace accountability: Hatim al-Ta'i
outline.gist: Strong law has not filled the gap. Hatim al-Ta'i, generous enough to slaughter his horse for a guest, lived for reputation: one ethic, not a system, and it does not work for most people. Every surah of this cluster has mentioned the Day.

outline.heading: Naqur: the blast that strikes the ear
outline.gist: Naqur is a sound that strikes the eardrum. At the first blast all die; the angel of death takes the trumpeter and then himself, Allah alone remains, then revives the trumpeter, whose second blast raises everyone.

outline.heading: A hard day even for the prophets
outline.gist: The day is hard for Muslims, non-Muslims and prophets alike; when people come to the prophets for help, they say only 'O Allah, grant safety'.

outline.heading: Not easy for the disbelievers
outline.gist: Saying it is not easy for the disbelievers implies, as scholars inferred, that it will be easier for others, though the day itself is hard.

outline.heading: Leave them to Me: when war criminals win prizes
outline.gist: As in Al-Muzzammil, Allah tells the Prophet to leave the arrogant to Him. When those who took countless lives receive Nobel prizes, these verses keep rage from consuming you.

outline.heading: Wahida: three readings, all correct
outline.gist: Allah created him alone without help; leave Me with him alone; or he was created alone. All three hold, and the word was chosen so that each does.

outline.heading: Recitation of the next verses
outline.gist: He recites the description of the man Allah created alone.

outline.heading: Wealth stretched out and sons present
outline.gist: Allah gave him abundant, lasting wealth, sons who testified to His generosity, and status. Understand verses generally first, then add the occasion of revelation.

outline.heading: Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, chief of Mecca
outline.gist: The father of Khalid was undisputedly Quraysh's top chief: led the rebuilding of the Ka'bah, brokered peace treaties, too senior to attend Abu Jahl's meetings. He died before the hijrah without accepting Islam.

outline.heading: Godfathers whose ring you must kiss
outline.gist: Every field has a figure behind the public face whose word no one breaks. Decide consciously whether you will kiss the ring rather than find out too late.

outline.heading: Uthman ibn Maz'un spared under al-Walid's protection
outline.gist: Returning early from Abyssinia on a false rumour that Mecca had accepted Islam, he alone was spared torture under al-Walid's protection, and it troubled him to be spared what his brothers and sisters suffered.

outline.heading: Labid's verse and the renounced protection
outline.gist: At a recital by Labid he affirmed 'everything besides Allah is false' but contradicted 'every bliss will end', since Paradise's does not. Told he could not be touched, he renounced al-Walid's protection.

outline.heading: An eye lost for Allah
outline.gist: Beaten until he lost an eye, he told al-Walid his good eye longed to suffer the same for Allah. He tells that the Prophet's hand restored the eye.

outline.heading: A leader's missed opportunity
outline.gist: Had al-Walid accepted the message, the seerah would read differently. Confused by the Quran's power, Quraysh came to him for guidance and he asked for time to think, the subject of the next verses.

outline.heading: Outro

30:55.ar: وَيَوۡمَ تَقُومُ ٱلسَّاعَةُ يُقۡسِمُ ٱلۡمُجۡرِمُونَ مَا لَبِثُواْ غَيۡرَ سَاعَةࣲۚ كَذَٰلِكَ كَانُواْ يُؤۡفَكُونَ
30:55.en: And the Day the Hour appears the criminals will swear they had remained but an hour. Thus they were deluded

30:56.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلۡعِلۡمَ وَٱلۡإِيمَٰنَ لَقَدۡ لَبِثۡتُمۡ فِي كِتَٰبِ ٱللَّهِ إِلَىٰ يَوۡمِ ٱلۡبَعۡثِۖ فَهَٰذَا يَوۡمُ ٱلۡبَعۡثِ وَلَٰكِنَّكُمۡ كُنتُمۡ لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
30:56.en: But those who were given knowledge and faith will say, "You remained the extent of Allah 's decree until the Day of Resurrection, and this is the Day of Resurrection, but you did not used to know

30:57.ar: فَيَوۡمَئِذࣲ لَّا يَنفَعُ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ مَعۡذِرَتُهُمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يُسۡتَعۡتَبُونَ
30:57.en: So that Day, their excuse will not benefit those who wronged, nor will they be asked to appease [Allah]

30:58.ar: وَلَقَدۡ ضَرَبۡنَا لِلنَّاسِ فِي هَٰذَا ٱلۡقُرۡءَانِ مِن كُلِّ مَثَلࣲۚ وَلَئِن جِئۡتَهُم بِـَٔايَةࣲ لَّيَقُولَنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓاْ إِنۡ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا مُبۡطِلُونَ
30:58.en: And We have certainly presented to the people in this Qur'an from every [kind of] example. But, [O Muhammad], if you should bring them a sign, the disbelievers will surely say, "You [believers] are but falsifiers

30:59.ar: كَذَٰلِكَ يَطۡبَعُ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
30:59.en: Thus does Allah seal the hearts of those who do not know

30:60.ar: فَٱصۡبِرۡ إِنَّ وَعۡدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقࣱّۖ وَلَا يَسۡتَخِفَّنَّكَ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يُوقِنُونَ
30:60.en: So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is truth. And let them not disquiet you who are not certain [in faith]

59:9.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ تَبَوَّءُو ٱلدَّارَ وَٱلۡإِيمَٰنَ مِن قَبۡلِهِمۡ يُحِبُّونَ مَنۡ هَاجَرَ إِلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا يَجِدُونَ فِي صُدُورِهِمۡ حَاجَةࣰ مِّمَّآ أُوتُواْ وَيُؤۡثِرُونَ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمۡ وَلَوۡ كَانَ بِهِمۡ خَصَاصَةࣱۚ وَمَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفۡسِهِۦ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡمُفۡلِحُونَ
59:9.en: And [also for] those who were settled in al-Madinah and [adopted] the faith before them. They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful

29:2.ar: أَحَسِبَ ٱلنَّاسُ أَن يُتۡرَكُوٓاْ أَن يَقُولُوٓاْ ءَامَنَّا وَهُمۡ لَا يُفۡتَنُونَ
29:2.en: Do the people think that they will be left to say, "We believe" and they will not be tried

9:107.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّخَذُواْ مَسۡجِدࣰ ا ضِرَارࣰ ا وَكُفۡرࣰ ا وَتَفۡرِيقَۢا بَيۡنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ وَإِرۡصَادࣰ ا لِّمَنۡ حَارَبَ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُۥ مِن قَبۡلُۚ وَلَيَحۡلِفُنَّ إِنۡ أَرَدۡنَآ إِلَّا ٱلۡحُسۡنَىٰۖ وَٱللَّهُ يَشۡهَدُ إِنَّهُمۡ لَكَٰذِبُونَ
9:107.en: And [there are] those [hypocrites] who took for themselves a mosque for causing harm and disbelief and division among the believers and as a station for whoever had warred against Allah and His Messenger before. And they will surely swear, "We intended only the best." And Allah testifies that indeed they are liars

9:108.ar: لَا تَقُمۡ فِيهِ أَبَدࣰ اۚ لَّمَسۡجِدٌ أُسِّسَ عَلَى ٱلتَّقۡوَىٰ مِنۡ أَوَّلِ يَوۡمٍ أَحَقُّ أَن تَقُومَ فِيهِۚ فِيهِ رِجَالࣱ يُحِبُّونَ أَن يَتَطَهَّرُواْۚ وَٱللَّهُ يُحِبُّ ٱلۡمُطَّهِّرِينَ
9:108.en: Do not stand [for prayer] within it - ever. A mosque founded on righteousness from the first day is more worthy for you to stand in. Within it are men who love to purify themselves; and Allah loves those who purify themselves

23:112.ar: قَٰلَ كَمۡ لَبِثۡتُمۡ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ عَدَدَ سِنِينَ
23:112.en: [Allah] will say, "How long did you remain on earth in number of years

23:113.ar: قَالُواْ لَبِثۡنَا يَوۡمًا أَوۡ بَعۡضَ يَوۡمࣲ فَسۡـَٔلِ ٱلۡعَآدِّينَ
23:113.en: They will say, "We remained a day or part of a day; ask those who enumerate

23:114.ar: قَٰلَ إِن لَّبِثۡتُمۡ إِلَّا قَلِيلࣰ اۖ لَّوۡ أَنَّكُمۡ كُنتُمۡ تَعۡلَمُونَ
23:114.en: He will say, "You stayed not but a little - if only you had known

20:104.ar: نَّحۡنُ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا يَقُولُونَ إِذۡ يَقُولُ أَمۡثَلُهُمۡ طَرِيقَةً إِن لَّبِثۡتُمۡ إِلَّا يَوۡمࣰ ا
20:104.en: We are most knowing of what they say when the best of them in manner will say, "You remained not but one day

17:88.ar: قُل لَّئِنِ ٱجۡتَمَعَتِ ٱلۡإِنسُ وَٱلۡجِنُّ عَلَىٰٓ أَن يَأۡتُواْ بِمِثۡلِ هَٰذَا ٱلۡقُرۡءَانِ لَا يَأۡتُونَ بِمِثۡلِهِۦ وَلَوۡ كَانَ بَعۡضُهُمۡ لِبَعۡضࣲ ظَهِيرࣰ ا
17:88.en: Say, "If mankind and the jinn gathered in order to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like of it, even if they were to each other assistants

28:49.ar: قُلۡ فَأۡتُواْ بِكِتَٰبࣲ مِّنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ هُوَ أَهۡدَىٰ مِنۡهُمَآ أَتَّبِعۡهُ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
28:49.en: Say, "Then bring a scripture from Allah which is more guiding than either of them that I may follow it, if you should be truthful

11:13.ar: أَمۡ يَقُولُونَ ٱفۡتَرَىٰهُۖ قُلۡ فَأۡتُواْ بِعَشۡرِ سُوَرࣲ مِّثۡلِهِۦ مُفۡتَرَيَٰتࣲ وَٱدۡعُواْ مَنِ ٱسۡتَطَعۡتُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
11:13.en: Or do they say, "He invented it"? Say, "Then bring ten surahs like it that have been invented and call upon [for assistance] whomever you can besides Allah, if you should be truthful

2:23.ar: وَإِن كُنتُمۡ فِي رَيۡبࣲ مِّمَّا نَزَّلۡنَا عَلَىٰ عَبۡدِنَا فَأۡتُواْ بِسُورَةࣲ مِّن مِّثۡلِهِۦ وَٱدۡعُواْ شُهَدَآءَكُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
2:23.en: And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our Servant [Muhammad], then produce a surah the like thereof and call upon your witnesses other than Allah, if you should be truthful

2:26.ar: ۞إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَسۡتَحۡيِۦٓ أَن يَضۡرِبَ مَثَلࣰ ا مَّا بَعُوضَةࣰ فَمَا فَوۡقَهَاۚ فَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ فَيَعۡلَمُونَ أَنَّهُ ٱلۡحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّهِمۡۖ وَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ فَيَقُولُونَ مَاذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِهَٰذَا مَثَلࣰ اۘ يُضِلُّ بِهِۦ كَثِيرࣰ ا وَيَهۡدِي بِهِۦ كَثِيرࣰ اۚ وَمَا يُضِلُّ بِهِۦٓ إِلَّا ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
2:26.en: Indeed, Allah is not timid to present an example - that of a mosquito or what is smaller than it. And those who have believed know that it is the truth from their Lord. But as for those who disbelieve, they say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?" He misleads many thereby and guides many thereby. And He misleads not except the defiantly disobedient

17:59.ar: وَمَا مَنَعَنَآ أَن نُّرۡسِلَ بِٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ إِلَّآ أَن كَذَّبَ بِهَا ٱلۡأَوَّلُونَۚ وَءَاتَيۡنَا ثَمُودَ ٱلنَّاقَةَ مُبۡصِرَةࣰ فَظَلَمُواْ بِهَاۚ وَمَا نُرۡسِلُ بِٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ إِلَّا تَخۡوِيفࣰ ا
17:59.en: And nothing has prevented Us from sending signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her. And We send not the signs except as a warning

43:51.ar: وَنَادَىٰ فِرۡعَوۡنُ فِي قَوۡمِهِۦ قَالَ يَٰقَوۡمِ أَلَيۡسَ لِي مُلۡكُ مِصۡرَ وَهَٰذِهِ ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُ تَجۡرِي مِن تَحۡتِيٓۚ أَفَلَا تُبۡصِرُونَ
43:51.en: And Pharaoh called out among his people; he said, "O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me; then do you not see

43:52.ar: أَمۡ أَنَا۠ خَيۡرࣱ مِّنۡ هَٰذَا ٱلَّذِي هُوَ مَهِينࣱ وَلَا يَكَادُ يُبِينُ
43:52.en: Or am I [not] better than this one who is insignificant and hardly makes himself clear

43:53.ar: فَلَوۡلَآ أُلۡقِيَ عَلَيۡهِ أَسۡوِرَةࣱ مِّن ذَهَبٍ أَوۡ جَآءَ مَعَهُ ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ مُقۡتَرِنِينَ
43:53.en: Then why have there not been placed upon him bracelets of gold or come with him the angels in conjunction

43:54.ar: فَٱسۡتَخَفَّ قَوۡمَهُۥ فَأَطَاعُوهُۚ إِنَّهُمۡ كَانُواْ قَوۡمࣰ ا فَٰسِقِينَ
43:54.en: So he bluffed his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were [themselves] a people defiantly disobedient [of Allah]

W8FmIFBaeQk.title: Arabic Tafsir: Closing Surat Ar-Rum (30:55-60) and Its Seventeen Laws
W8FmIFBaeQk.one_line: The end of Ar-Rum: laws to use, overcome or accept, the wrongdoers who think life lasted an hour, patience, and seventeen laws drawn from the surah.
W8FmIFBaeQk.summary: He sorts Allah's laws into three kinds: those you use for your benefit, such as cause and effect and effort, those of human nature you must overcome, as heroes do when they stand firm against the instinct to flee, and those you can only accept, like the cycle of weakness and strength. Other nations respect these laws without crediting Allah, while Muslims credit Allah and ignore them, preferring slogans and wishes for thunderbolts to the tireless work of the companions. He recaps the section on relationships and stresses that every relationship, marriage included, needs clear duties and expectations. In the closing verses, the wrongdoers who broke Allah's laws claim they lived only an hour. Those given knowledge and faith reply that what matters is not the length of life but whether you did what was asked in the span Allah decreed. Being turned from truth begins with exempting yourself from a law, whether a state claiming its ends justify killing civilians or a person who parks in the middle of the road. Allah gave every kind of parable, while miracles never convinced those set on refusing. The surah closes with patience, meaning persistent striving, and a warning not to let people without certainty make you take the truth lightly. He ends by listing seventeen laws from the surah.

9Mc2xz-8cXk.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Hastiness and Argumentativeness
9Mc2xz-8cXk.one_line: Two traits the Quran says to change: hastiness, cured by patience and gratitude, and argumentativeness, cured by listening and letting go of being right.
9Mc2xz-8cXk.summary: He begins with Gaza: the starvation is a man-made atrocity, and what he feels beyond sorrow is embarrassment at his own helplessness, a lesson the youth must carry so that in their generation this is no longer possible. The series' premise follows: the Quran names human traits not to shame but to change, against a culture, Western and Middle Eastern, that accepts people 'as they are' and lets a man excuse hitting his wife with 'I lose my temper'. The first trait is haste. Man was created of it and prays for what harms him, though nothing of value comes without the tax of patience; Allah took six days for our sake. The Prophet praised the forbearance and deliberateness of Ashajj and rebuked the tortured Khabbab's 'until when?' with 'you are hasty'. Perseverance and gratitude together answer most of the Quran's list of flaws. The second trait is argumentativeness: man argues more than anything, the quarrelsome are hated by Allah, and nations lost guidance through argument. He asks people to listen, sleep on criticism, accept being wrong, discuss to learn rather than win, and walk away from those who only want to argue, as the Prophet did with Utbah and with the man who claimed 'something better'.

outline.heading: Opening
Gaza: a man-made atrocity
outline.gist: Israel's brutality has passed any limit its defenders can excuse. A hurricane or earthquake is nature; starving and killing a people while the world watches is a man-made atrocity, a sign that we are marching towards the end of times.

outline.heading: The embarrassment of helplessness
outline.gist: Beyond the sorrow, what comes over him is embarrassment: people who look and think like him are in pain and he has no pull, no voice, and nothing to offer that matches the guidance, numbers and feeling of the ummah.

outline.heading: The lesson for the next generation
outline.gist: His generation reached adulthood without the ability to stop this and will carry that. The young must choose and build better so that by the time they are in his place it is no longer possible, planning for the long haul rather than short-term reactions.

outline.heading: Created traits are meant to change, not to excuse
outline.gist: For the coming weeks: traits you were created with, nothing to be ashamed of, but things you must adjust. The Quran describes both how we are and the potential to change, against today's culture of accepting people as they are. The man who breaks things, hurts his children and hits his wife and then says 'I lose my temper' has no get-out-of-jail card; changing it is the point of his existence.

outline.heading: Man was created hasty
outline.gist: Al-Anbiya: man was created of haste, so do not ask Me to hurry My signs. Al-Isra: he prays for evil as he prays for good, because he wants what he wants now even when it will harm him.

outline.heading: Nothing worth having comes fast
outline.gist: Nothing of value comes without the tax of patience. Instant meals, thirty-day languages and love at first sight are nonsense; whatever came easily was either cheated or a starter kit for something harder. Allah created the heavens and earth in six days though He needed none; we are the ones who needed to learn that value takes time.

outline.heading: Ashajj: forbearance and deliberateness
outline.gist: The Prophet told Ashajj Abd al-Qays that he had two traits Allah and His Messenger love, forbearance and taking things slowly. Asked whether they were acquired or innate, he said Allah created him so, and Ashajj praised Allah for it.

outline.heading: Khabbab: "you are hasty"
outline.gist: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, laid on his own blacksmith's coals until he could not walk, crawled to the Prophet and asked 'until when?'. The Prophet answered sternly that those before them suffered worse, that Allah would complete this matter, but that they were hasty.

outline.heading: Perseverance and gratitude answer most flaws
outline.gist: The opposite of haste is patience and perseverance. Most of the negative traits the Quran lists have only a few opposites, chiefly perseverance and gratitude; have those two and you can omit half the list.

outline.heading: Haste was needed to survive; now tame it
outline.gist: We are evolutionarily hasty like all mammals: in the Serengeti an animal that is not in a hurry dies. We no longer need it that way, so we have to learn to tame it.

outline.heading: Interlude
Man, the most argumentative creation
outline.gist: Al-Kahf, recited every Friday: man argues more than anything. After the creation of the heavens and earth, man created from a drop raises his head and starts arguing, forgetting how weak and ignorant he began.

outline.heading: The quarrelsome and the peoples who lost guidance
outline.gist: The most hated to Allah is the relentlessly quarrelsome; no people lost their guidance except by becoming argumentative. Some argue with no substance, only for the love of it, whether they are right or not.

outline.heading: Put it down and listen
outline.gist: The ummah has argued some questions for a thousand years. Listen, mull it over for a day, sleep on it. Faith built only on arguing is not trustworthy; it is reached through reflection, and no one who always argues back can take feedback or improve.

outline.heading: Defending a mistake only you know about
outline.gist: We know our own mistake before anyone else and start building the argument to win when someone confronts us. Try listening and accepting instead; it is refreshing to meet, and to be, someone who does.

outline.heading: The Prophet accepted correction in public
outline.gist: Many of the world's conflicts are two parties with no interest in hearing each other. The Prophet listened deeply and took feedback, even publicly: the Quran asked him why he gave leave to those who sought to stay behind from battle, for everyone to hear.

outline.heading: What listening gains
outline.gist: Understanding where someone comes from is a win even without agreement: a new angle, a better grasp of the problem, a way to hold yourself to your beliefs. If everyone only argues, no one changes; we expect non-Muslims to listen while refusing to listen ourselves. Both haste and argument are human nature; the shame is not changing them.

outline.heading: Being right is overrated
outline.gist: Being right means nothing, as the married know. Being wrong is easier and people who accept being wrong keep learning; those who must always be right stop growing.

outline.heading: "I'm good": the 300 messages
outline.gist: Do not argue, and if you must, say kind things; to someone who only wants to argue, just say 'I'm good'. People bring him hundreds of text messages to judge who won; he would rather jump from a plane, because self-worth is not tied to winning.

outline.heading: Discuss to learn: the Prophet let Utbah finish
outline.gist: Discuss to learn and share, not to win. Utbah came with absurd offers of a cure, wealth, kingship and women; the Prophet let him speak to the end, then asked to be heard in turn.

outline.heading: The man with something better
outline.gist: A man said he had something better than what the Prophet had. The Prophet listened, called it beautiful, then recited Quran until the man conceded it was better and left. Most of the time we do not even know what we are arguing about.

outline.heading: Outro

2:264.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ لَا تُبۡطِلُواْ صَدَقَٰتِكُم بِٱلۡمَنِّ وَٱلۡأَذَىٰ كَٱلَّذِي يُنفِقُ مَالَهُۥ رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَا يُؤۡمِنُ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡيَوۡمِ ٱلۡأٓخِرِۖ فَمَثَلُهُۥ كَمَثَلِ صَفۡوَانٍ عَلَيۡهِ تُرَابࣱ فَأَصَابَهُۥ وَابِلࣱ فَتَرَكَهُۥ صَلۡدࣰ اۖ لَّا يَقۡدِرُونَ عَلَىٰ شَيۡءࣲ مِّمَّا كَسَبُواْۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ
2:264.en: O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury as does one who spends his wealth [only] to be seen by the people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is like that of a [large] smooth stone upon which is dust and is hit by a downpour that leaves it bare. They are unable [to keep] anything of what they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people

d-mMyrHx2PM.speaker: adnan
d-mMyrHx2PM.speaker_note: Continues his own series ('a number of paradigms over the last few weeks'), speaks of leaving the Middle East for the West, and delivers the Arabic second khutbah in the same voice.
d-mMyrHx2PM.title: The Quran's Outcomes for Character: Disloyalty and Ungratefulness
d-mMyrHx2PM.one_line: Kafur and kanud: man begs Allah in hardship, forgets Him in ease, and repays endless gifts with nothing, unlike the loyal war horse.
d-mMyrHx2PM.summary: Two years after October 7, with Gaza celebrating some relief, he asks the community to reflect, admits he is not ready to speak about it, and notes that Western Muslims, himself included, are the most privileged alive. He then takes two Quranic traits treated almost as one: kufr in its root sense of covering up a blessing, and kanud, the word Arabs used for land that yields nothing however much it is watered. The man of Surah Yunus prays lying down, sitting and standing, then walks on as though he never prayed; the passengers of Al-Isra forget every rival on the stormy sea and turn away once on land; the one given life and death is still ungrateful. The war horses of Al-Adiyat charge panting into a death trap out of loyalty to a master who gave them a little food and water, yet man, given incomparably more by his Lord, gives nothing back, knows it, and only wants more; the graves will be overturned and what the hearts hid exposed. The Arabic second khutbah restates this: most Quranic uses of kufr mean denial of blessings, and these traits can be changed. The Prophet modelled the cure: standing in night prayer as thanks, never reminding anyone of a favour, and publicly acknowledging Abu Bakr's generosity he could not repay.

outline.heading: Opening
Two years after October 7
outline.gist: After reciting Yunus 12, he pauses on Gaza: no one thought it would last two years. People who lived under bombardment are celebrating a little normality and some peace while the rest of the world thrives. He is not ready to analyse it, but asks everyone to reflect on how things were before October 2023, though nothing should have been any different since 1945.

outline.heading: The most privileged Muslims on the planet
outline.gist: Muslims in the West are the most privileged Muslims alive. He grew up in the Middle East and would never have left by choice, but living here has shown him how privileged he is.

outline.heading: Flaws named so that we change
outline.gist: The Quran points out our natural flaws not to shame us but so we learn and transform. After several such traits in past weeks, today's pair is disloyalty and ungratefulness, which the Quran treats as one; he separates them only for reflection.

outline.heading: Yunus 12: he walks on as if he never prayed
outline.gist: Harm is the loss of a loved one, wealth, status or opportunity. In it man prays lying down, sitting and standing; once relieved he 'passes by', a striking image, as if he had never called. So are the deeds of the transgressors made attractive to them.

outline.heading: Kafur: covering up the gift
outline.gist: Al-Isra: at sea every rival vanishes and only He is called; safe on land, man turns away, ever kafur. Most Quranic uses of the word mean ingratitude, about 80% in his count. The root means to cover, which is why so many Middle Eastern villages carry the name Kafr: instead of declaring a gift and its giver, we cover it up so we never have to think of it again.

outline.heading: Disloyalty to the One who gave you life
outline.gist: Kufr became the word for disbelief because it is disloyalty to the One who put you here. He gives you life, death and life again, and still man is ungrateful: we enjoy what we get with no thought of where it came from and no interest in paying it back.

outline.heading: Al-Adiyat: the charging war horses
outline.gist: Allah swears by the horses that charge panting, strike sparks from the rock, raid at dawn, raise the dust and plunge into the midst of the enemy.

outline.heading: Why the horse runs into death
outline.gist: Why would a horse get up before dawn and run full speed into a death trap? Because you fed it a little food and water. For that it loves you enough to run, breathe and strike as hard as it can into the enemy's ranks.

outline.heading: Kanud: land that yields nothing
outline.gist: Man is kanud to his Lord. The Arabs used the word for land that produces nothing however much water you pour on it; it has almost no other usage or derivatives. Allah gives us everything and we give Him nothing back.

outline.heading: He is witness to it, and wants only more
outline.gist: Man knows it and bears witness to it: how much he was given and how little he gave, how often he was rescued and how rarely he thanked. Yet his love of more is intense; he just wants more.

outline.heading: The graves overturned, the hearts exposed
outline.gist: When the graves are overturned and what is in the breasts is brought out, his Lord will lay it all open: what We did for you and what you did, how We treated you and how you treated Us. You do not have to be like that.

outline.heading: Interlude
Traits to shed: kafur and kanud
outline.gist: The Quran came to change souls: Allah strengthens the fitrah He loves and asks us to shed other instincts and replace them with better ones. Man is kafur, denying Allah's blessings, and kanud, with little loyalty to his Lord, wanting much and giving little, never thanking or remembering the gift. Most Quranic uses of kufr mean denial of a blessing; denying the blessing of life and existence itself is the kufr of disbelief.

outline.heading: The horse is more loyal than man
outline.gist: Rescued at sea, man turns away. The horse is not stupid: it knows it is going to its slaughter, yet it loves the master who fed it scraps and water, and answers 'to death for your sake'. Who gave more, that man to his horse or our Lord to us? Why is man barren land that yields nothing however much is poured on it? These are traits he can change if he wants.

outline.heading: "Should I not be a grateful servant?"
outline.gist: Whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah. Aisha asked why he stood so long in prayer when Allah had forgiven his past and future sins; he answered that he showed gratitude by standing and speaking to Him. We, once we get what we prayed for, forget for months that we ever made dua; he was not like that.

outline.heading: He never reminded anyone of a favour
outline.gist: Do not void your charity with reminders and hurt. He gave and walked away, never reminding anyone of what he had done, and when someone brought up his favour he would ask them to stop; the Quran taught him to be grateful to everyone.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr's favour left to Allah
outline.gist: Just before he died he said he had repaid every favour done to him except Abu Bakr's, which he could not repay and left to Allah, and he ordered every small door into the masjid closed except Abu Bakr's. Look up these words in the Quran and see how Allah shifts our behaviour.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Palestine, Gaza and the suffering of Muslims
themes.note: Two years into a war no one expected to last, Gaza celebrates some relief while the world thrives around it. He is not ready to analyse it but asks everyone to reflect on how things were before October 2023, though nothing should have been different since the occupation began.

themes.label: Muslim identity and life in the West / Canada
themes.note: Muslims in the West are the most privileged Muslims on the planet. He would never have left the Middle East by choice, but living here taught him how privileged he is.

themes.label: Character and manners (akhlaq)
themes.note: The Quran points out natural human flaws not to shame people but so they learn and transform; the series has covered several such paradigms and now turns to ingratitude and disloyalty.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation
themes.note: Ingratitude is the human default: pray in hardship, walk on in ease, forget who answered. Kufr at root means covering up a gift instead of acknowledging its giver; man takes everything with no thought of where it came from and no will to pay back, and on the Day what the hearts concealed will be exposed.

themes.label: Methodology: how to read texts, tafsir method, intellectual approach
themes.note: He argues from root meanings: k-f-r as covering (hence village names), kanud as the word for barren land with almost no other usage, and the claim that most Quranic uses of kufr mean denial of blessings rather than disbelief.

themes.label: Oaths, promises, trust and loyalty
themes.note: Loyalty is the measure: a horse runs into a death trap for a master who fed it a little, while man, given life and everything else by his Lord, gives nothing back and only wants more. Kanud is the absence of wafa and wala toward Allah.

themes.label: Gratitude (shukr) and appreciation
themes.note: Arabic restatement: man wants much, gives little, never thanks, praises or remembers the gift. The cure is in the Prophet's example: thank people, show gratitude in worship, never remind anyone of your favours, acknowledge theirs.

themes.label: The Prophet's attributes, character and example
themes.note: He stood in night prayer as gratitude even after being forgiven, never reminded people of what he did for them, and publicly honoured Abu Bakr's generosity he could not repay, leaving the reward to Allah and keeping only Abu Bakr's door into the masjid open.

quran.point: Recited as the opening text and explained from 8:15: man prays lying, sitting and standing in harm, then walks on as if he never called; thus the transgressors' deeds are made attractive to them.
At sea all you call upon vanish except Him; brought safe to land you turn away; man is ever ungrateful (kafur). Repeated in the Arabic khutbah at 23:31.
He gave you life, will give you death, then life again; indeed man is ungrateful.
The charging, panting horses striking sparks, raiding at dawn, raising dust and plunging into the enemy's midst: loyalty to a master who merely fed them.
Man is kanud to his Lord, barren land that returns nothing; he is a witness to it; he is intense in his love of wealth and of more.
When the graves are overturned and what is in the breasts brought out, their Lord is fully aware: the day the ledger of what He gave and what we gave is exposed.
Aisha cites Allah's forgiveness of the Prophet's past and future sins to ask why he still stands so long in prayer.
Do not nullify your charity with reminders and hurt; the Prophet never reminded anyone of a favour.

hadith.gist: Whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah.
Aisha asked why he stood in prayer until his feet swelled when Allah had forgiven him; he replied: should I not love to be a grateful servant?
Shortly before his death the Prophet said no one had done him a favour he had not repaid except Abu Bakr, whose favour he could not repay and so left to Allah.
He ordered every private door opening into the masjid closed except Abu Bakr's.

maxims: Kufr is covering up a gift
Kanud: land that yields nothing however much you water it
A horse is more loyal to its master than man to Allah
He wants much and gives little
Not to shame us, but so we may change

takeaways: When relief comes, do not walk on as if you never prayed; remember who answered and stay as attached in ease as in hardship.
Acknowledge your gifts and their giver openly instead of covering them up, and thank the people who helped you, since not thanking people is not thanking Allah.
Express gratitude in action, as the Prophet did by standing in night prayer after being forgiven.
Give Allah loyalty proportionate to what you receive; be at least as faithful as a horse to the one who feeds it.
Never remind people of favours you did them; repay favours done to you and leave what you cannot repay to Allah.

73:20.ar: ۞إِنَّ رَبَّكَ يَعۡلَمُ أَنَّكَ تَقُومُ أَدۡنَىٰ مِن ثُلُثَيِ ٱلَّيۡلِ وَنِصۡفَهُۥ وَثُلُثَهُۥ وَطَآئِفَةࣱ مِّنَ ٱلَّذِينَ مَعَكَۚ وَٱللَّهُ يُقَدِّرُ ٱلَّيۡلَ وَٱلنَّهَارَۚ عَلِمَ أَن لَّن تُحۡصُوهُ فَتَابَ عَلَيۡكُمۡۖ فَٱقۡرَءُواْ مَا تَيَسَّرَ مِنَ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانِۚ عَلِمَ أَن سَيَكُونُ مِنكُم مَّرۡضَىٰ وَءَاخَرُونَ يَضۡرِبُونَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ يَبۡتَغُونَ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ وَءَاخَرُونَ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِۖ فَٱقۡرَءُواْ مَا تَيَسَّرَ مِنۡهُۚ وَأَقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتُواْ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَأَقۡرِضُواْ ٱللَّهَ قَرۡضًا حَسَنࣰ اۚ وَمَا تُقَدِّمُواْ لِأَنفُسِكُم مِّنۡ خَيۡرࣲ تَجِدُوهُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ هُوَ خَيۡرࣰ ا وَأَعۡظَمَ أَجۡرࣰ اۚ وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرُواْ ٱللَّهَۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمُۢ
73:20.en: Indeed, your Lord knows, [O Muhammad], that you stand [in prayer] almost two thirds of the night or half of it or a third of it, and [so do] a group of those with you. And Allah determines [the extent of] the night and the day. He has known that you [Muslims] will not be able to do it and has turned to you in forgiveness, so recite what is easy [for you] of the Qur'an. He has known that there will be among you those who are ill and others traveling throughout the land seeking [something] of the bounty of Allah and others fighting for the cause of Allah. So recite what is easy from it and establish prayer and give zakah and loan Allah a goodly loan. And whatever good you put forward for yourselves - you will find it with Allah. It is better and greater in reward. And seek forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful

73:1.en: O you who wraps himself [in clothing]

73:2.en: Arise [to pray] the night, except for a little

73:3.en: Half of it - or subtract from it a little

73:4.ar: أَوۡ زِدۡ عَلَيۡهِ وَرَتِّلِ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ تَرۡتِيلًا
73:4.en: Or add to it, and recite the Qur'an with measured recitation

73:5.ar: إِنَّا سَنُلۡقِي عَلَيۡكَ قَوۡلࣰ ا ثَقِيلًا
73:5.en: Indeed, We will cast upon you a heavy word

73:6.ar: إِنَّ نَاشِئَةَ ٱلَّيۡلِ هِيَ أَشَدُّ وَطۡـࣰٔ ا وَأَقۡوَمُ قِيلًا
73:6.en: Indeed, the hours of the night are more effective for concurrence [of heart and tongue] and more suitable for words

73:7.ar: إِنَّ لَكَ فِي ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبۡحࣰ ا طَوِيلࣰ ا
73:7.en: Indeed, for you by day is prolonged occupation

73:8.ar: وَٱذۡكُرِ ٱسۡمَ رَبِّكَ وَتَبَتَّلۡ إِلَيۡهِ تَبۡتِيلࣰ ا
73:8.en: And remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with [complete] devotion

73:9.ar: رَّبُّ ٱلۡمَشۡرِقِ وَٱلۡمَغۡرِبِ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ فَٱتَّخِذۡهُ وَكِيلࣰ ا
73:9.en: [He is] the Lord of the East and the West; there is no deity except Him, so take Him as Disposer of [your] affairs

73:10.ar: وَٱصۡبِرۡ عَلَىٰ مَا يَقُولُونَ وَٱهۡجُرۡهُمۡ هَجۡرࣰ ا جَمِيلࣰ ا
73:10.en: And be patient over what they say and avoid them with gracious avoidance

73:11.ar: وَذَرۡنِي وَٱلۡمُكَذِّبِينَ أُوْلِي ٱلنَّعۡمَةِ وَمَهِّلۡهُمۡ قَلِيلًا
73:11.en: And leave Me with [the matter of] the deniers, those of ease [in life], and allow them respite a little

73:12.ar: إِنَّ لَدَيۡنَآ أَنكَالࣰ ا وَجَحِيمࣰ ا
73:12.en: Indeed, with Us [for them] are shackles and burning fire

73:13.ar: وَطَعَامࣰ ا ذَا غُصَّةࣲ وَعَذَابًا أَلِيمࣰ ا
73:13.en: And food that chokes and a painful punishment

73:14.ar: يَوۡمَ تَرۡجُفُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ وَٱلۡجِبَالُ وَكَانَتِ ٱلۡجِبَالُ كَثِيبࣰ ا مَّهِيلًا
73:14.en: On the Day the earth and the mountains will convulse and the mountains will become a heap of sand pouring down

73:15.ar: إِنَّآ أَرۡسَلۡنَآ إِلَيۡكُمۡ رَسُولࣰ ا شَٰهِدًا عَلَيۡكُمۡ كَمَآ أَرۡسَلۡنَآ إِلَىٰ فِرۡعَوۡنَ رَسُولࣰ ا
73:15.en: Indeed, We have sent to you a Messenger as a witness upon you just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger

73:16.ar: فَعَصَىٰ فِرۡعَوۡنُ ٱلرَّسُولَ فَأَخَذۡنَٰهُ أَخۡذࣰ ا وَبِيلࣰ ا
73:16.en: But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger, so We seized him with a ruinous seizure

73:17.ar: فَكَيۡفَ تَتَّقُونَ إِن كَفَرۡتُمۡ يَوۡمࣰ ا يَجۡعَلُ ٱلۡوِلۡدَٰنَ شِيبًا
73:17.en: Then how can you fear, if you disbelieve, a Day that will make the children white- haired

73:18.ar: ٱلسَّمَآءُ مُنفَطِرُۢ بِهِۦۚ كَانَ وَعۡدُهُۥ مَفۡعُولًا
73:18.en: The heaven will break apart therefrom; ever is His promise fulfilled

73:19.ar: إِنَّ هَٰذِهِۦ تَذۡكِرَةࣱۖ فَمَن شَآءَ ٱتَّخَذَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِۦ سَبِيلًا
73:19.en: Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way

48:2.ar: لِّيَغۡفِرَ لَكَ ٱللَّهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِن ذَنۢبِكَ وَمَا تَأَخَّرَ وَيُتِمَّ نِعۡمَتَهُۥ عَلَيۡكَ وَيَهۡدِيَكَ صِرَٰطࣰ ا مُّسۡتَقِيمࣰ ا
48:2.en: That Allah may forgive for you what preceded of your sin and what will follow and complete His favor upon you and guide you to a straight path

DVkMRJOecpw.speaker: adnan
DVkMRJOecpw.speaker_note: Single voice continuing his Al-Muzzammil series; refers to what he tells people in Ramadan and to his own work with worried congregants
DVkMRJOecpw.title: Surat Al-Muzzammil, Part 4: Verse 20 (Part 2)
DVkMRJOecpw.one_line: The closing verse of Al-Muzzammil: Allah's excuses for imperfect worship, the bare minimum of recitation, a goodly loan, and ending with forgiveness.
DVkMRJOecpw.summary: He finishes the long final verse of Al-Muzzammil. After fifteen years of demanding night prayer, Allah tells the companions He knows they could not keep it up, and offers three excuses: illness, travel to earn a living, and fighting in His cause. The real goal was never the hours or the number of rak'ahs but a fixed commitment to reciting the Quran, so the believer should settle on an amount and keep it through every fluctuation. He contrasts this with how anxious people are about whether they do enough, and with the Prophet standing until his feet swelled out of gratitude. To make up for the shortfall, Allah asks for prayer as one is able, zakah, and an extra goodly loan, which He alone repays with increase; generosity covers flaws, as Imam al-Shafi'i put it. Every good deed is sent ahead for oneself and will be found with Allah, recognisable but greater. The verse then ends, not with judgment, but with a command to seek forgiveness, because Allah gains nothing from our deeds, excuses our failures and still rewards us. He calls the nine commands of the surah gifts that build an inner core life will test.

outline.heading: Third comment: illness, travel for a living, fighting
outline.gist: Allah knew some would be sick, some travelling and working long hours to earn a living, and some in combat for His sake, so they could not pray all night. Again the point is a committed amount of recitation.

outline.heading: After fifteen years: night prayer already held the other commands
outline.gist: Qiyam contains recitation, devotion and the rest of the commands within it. Fifteen years after giving it, Allah explains why it is fine that the companions did not do it all perfectly.

outline.heading: People worry whether they do enough; Allah's three understandings
outline.gist: A worry he meets daily in his work. Allah says He knows the night and day fluctuate, that you cannot keep count, and that your state will not stay the same: sickness, long hours on call, combat.

outline.heading: Forget the clock: eight or twenty rak'ahs makes no difference
outline.gist: Twice the verse returns to recitation. That is why he tells people in Ramadan the number of rak'ahs does not matter: commit to an amount, such as a juz, within your prayer every night as you are able.

outline.heading: No shaming: the optimal set and the bare minimum
outline.gist: He has never seen a commander offer his followers so many excuses. Instead of 'shame on you' there is understanding; Allah gave the optimal set of commands and then the bare minimum: make sure you recite.

outline.heading: The Prophet's swollen feet: should I not be a grateful servant?
outline.gist: The Prophet worried whether he did enough and stood until his feet swelled; when Aishah reminded him Allah had forgiven his sins, he asked whether he should not then be a grateful servant. The verse eases that worry: keep Quran in your life.

outline.heading: Establish prayer, give zakah, lend Allah a goodly loan
outline.gist: After reciting the verse's final commands he explains them: pray as best you can, give zakah from your wealth, and then offer Allah something more, a loan you will collect on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: The only lender who repays with increase; giving makes up the shortfall
outline.gist: Everyone else must return a loan exactly, yet Allah repays with increase while removing blessing from riba. Since no one can perfect the commands, giving compensates for a lack of commitment.

outline.heading: Imam al-Shafi'i: shield yourself with generosity
outline.gist: Young people should read al-Shafi'i's small, authentically attributed diwan. One line: protect yourself with generosity, because generosity has always covered every flaw.

outline.heading: Generosity covers every flaw, even a husband's
outline.gist: A man you cannot imagine anyone tolerating is forgiven much if he is generous with his time, heart, love and wallet. So with Allah: give, and it covers the variability, mistakes and lapses of focus.

outline.heading: Whatever good you send ahead, you send for yourselves
outline.gist: One of the most perfect phrases in Arabic: what you offer, you offer to yourselves. Every command in the surah is for you; Allah gets nothing from any of it, and whoever teaches or listens about Him benefits.

outline.heading: You will find it with Allah: recognisable, but greater
outline.gist: Tajiduhu means you will find the deed as it was, the money, time, love and effort you gave, and recognise it as yours, yet bigger and carrying more reward than you thought possible.

outline.heading: Seek forgiveness: left for last, after accountability
outline.gist: Istighfar is missing from the first page and saved for the end, after the review: you did not do it well, there are reasons, He excuses you, accepts the small deed and enlarges it, so seek His forgiveness.

outline.heading: The ninth command and the servant's embarrassment
outline.gist: The other commands were repeats; this one is new. He commands what only benefits you, you fall short, and He still excuses and rewards you: that should embarrass you into admitting the flaw. He is Forgiving and Merciful, and our best will never be good enough.

outline.heading: The verse brings it together: gifts for the core, accountability with forgiveness
outline.gist: All nine commands are gifts that strengthen a core you will need, because life will test it hard. Where accountability would bring judgment, this verse pairs it with forgiveness.

outline.heading: Next, Al-Muddaththir: the outward face of the same coin
outline.gist: With the requirements, ethics, spirituality and behaviour in place, Al-Muzzammil gives what you carry inside; Al-Muddaththir, the other face of the coin, covers what you do on the outside.

yl_I6Qu-N-4.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Luqman, Idle Talk, Keeping It Simple and the Gift of Wisdom (31:6-12)
yl_I6Qu-N-4.one_line: Young people who buy idle talk need simple, achievable guidance from wise elders, just as Allah sums up faith and creation in a few words.
yl_I6Qu-N-4.summary: Surat Luqman is about the relationship between generations, and since wisdom sits mostly with elders, they carry responsibility for it, as Umar told a father who complained of his son. 'Idle talk' covers far more than music: anything useless bought with money and time, from empty lectures to screens, smoking and pointless spending, typical of youth who take everything as a joke and turn away as if deaf. Maturity means taking things seriously. Allah's response is striking: the shortest description of the people of Paradise in the Quran, simply faith and good deeds. He draws a method from this: elders often demand a perfection they never had; with a struggling young person, keep demands simple and set them up to succeed, thank them for avoiding the major sins and build from there, like the Prophet with the Bedouin who would add nothing. A survey of his Islamic school students who answered that everything is haram shows how heavy religion can feel. Allah's argument for Himself is equally simple: sky, earth, life and rain in one verse, with the challenge to show what anything else created. Luqman is introduced only as given wisdom, which is scarce today even though information is everywhere; without it knowledge produces extremism or laxity.

outline.heading: A surah about the generations
outline.gist: Luqman deals with the bond between old and young, parents and children, a theme it shares only with Surat Maryam.

outline.heading: Wisdom puts the responsibility on elders
outline.gist: Elders hold most of the wisdom, so they are responsible for building the relationship; the young are rarely to blame.

outline.heading: Umar: you wronged him before he wronged you
outline.gist: A father complained of his son, who said he was given a poor mother, no teaching and a bad name; Umar blamed the father.

outline.heading: Prayer, zakat and certainty in the Hereafter
outline.gist: Prayer stands for worship between you and Allah, zakat for worship that benefits others, and certainty in the Hereafter is the glue that gives them meaning.

outline.heading: Recitation of verses 6-7
Idle talk is broader than music
outline.gist: Lahw al-hadith is any speech without benefit, even a useless lecture; lahw is something lesser that distracts from something more important.

outline.heading: Distraction from what matters
outline.gist: Being distracted from prayer is the problem whatever distracted you, except genuine excuses like a surgeon mid-operation.

outline.heading: 'Buys': paying to be misled
outline.gist: He spends money and effort on what misleads him, out of ignorance, and treats it all as a joke.

outline.heading: A humiliating punishment, and what 'Our signs' means
outline.gist: He is humiliated by wasted youth or at the Reckoning; the signs recited include the signs in creation that prophets teach.

outline.heading: Turning away as if deaf
outline.gist: He hears but acts as though his ears were plugged; his arrogance is toward listening, not toward the speaker.

outline.heading: A portrait of many young people
outline.gist: Most of us were like this once: money spent on gyms, aimless travel and screens that only add distraction.

outline.heading: Smoking and the rest: whatever does not benefit harms
outline.gist: Lahw is general so it covers the useless as well as the harmful; most people outgrow it with age, though some never do.

outline.heading: Maturity means taking things seriously
outline.gist: Muru'ah, not physical puberty, separates a man from a boy: a child laughing at a funeral is excused, an adult is not.

outline.heading: Why talking to them feels like talking to the deaf
outline.gist: In an adult this deserves punishment, but among the young it is common and points to a lack of wisdom.

outline.heading: Recitation of verses 8-11
The shortest description of the people of Paradise
outline.gist: Elsewhere the Quran lists many traits; here only faith and good deeds, because complexity pushes this listener away.

outline.heading: Elders demand a perfection they never had
outline.gist: A harsh elder is silenced when someone twenty years older walks in who remembers him as a youth.

outline.heading: Keep it simple and do not set them up to fail
outline.gist: 'Do what you can of what I command'; asking the unready for everything guarantees failure, like a student placed in a class he cannot follow.

outline.heading: Set them up to succeed
outline.gist: The educator's task is to create conditions for success, not to quote the long lists of Al-Mu'minun or Al-Ma'arij at someone still lost.

outline.heading: Ask for the basics, then add
outline.gist: Thank him for avoiding zina and alcohol, build on Jumu'ah; the Prophet said of the Bedouin who would add nothing, 'he succeeds if truthful'.

outline.heading: A tenth of the commands may save some
outline.gist: The Prophet said a time would come when holding to a tenth saves; he warns we are not yet in that time and people's capacities differ.

outline.heading: 'Everything is haram': a classroom survey
outline.gist: Over four years about 60% of his students answered 'everything'; half joking, it revealed how they feel about the religion.

outline.heading: Heavens without pillars you can see
outline.gist: If you cannot see what holds the sky up, you are surrounded by things you do not grasp; do not demand full understanding from others.

outline.heading: Mountains as anchors so the earth does not sway
outline.gist: Rawasi are ship anchors; most of a mountain lies below ground and steadies the earth.

outline.heading: Creatures, rain and plants in one verse
outline.gist: What Ar-Ra'd and Al-An'am describe at length is compressed here into a single verse covering sky, earth, life and its food.

outline.heading: 'Show me what others besides Him created'
outline.gist: Humans only remix what Allah made, with a hundred disasters before one useful result.

outline.heading: The simplest argument for God
outline.gist: Persuasion should be short too; compared with Ibrahim's star argument or the debates in Saba, Luqman's case takes two lines.

outline.heading: Four things you know; worship their Creator
outline.gist: Sky above, steady earth, life and rain-fed food; take one away and you die. Worship the One who made them, even if you do not know His name.

outline.heading: The wrongdoers know they are astray
outline.gist: Their misguidance is plain and needs no long debate.

outline.heading: The first page prepares for Luqman's simple advice
outline.gist: Luqman's words follow the same method: wisdom, guidance, mercy and simplicity; he likely lived in Dawud's era and taught his people in Africa.

outline.heading: Memorise the page of Luqman
outline.gist: It will serve you as a young person hearing a caring elder and as an elder speaking to others.

outline.heading: Recitation of verse 12
Luqman introduced only as given wisdom
outline.gist: Surahs were named after revelation; Luqman appears nowhere else, and Allah does not even say whether he was a prophet.

outline.heading: What wisdom is
outline.gist: Hard to define; teaching it is one of the prophets' tasks, and it means knowing how to act on what is right.

outline.heading: Information is everywhere, wisdom is scarce
outline.gist: AI on the phone answers anything, but without wisdom knowledge produces extremists who harm people or lax people with no limits.

outline.heading: Like medicine, religion is learned by practice
outline.gist: All medical facts are online, yet doctors train for years at the bedside; the Prophet showed us how to apply the deen.

outline.heading: Outro

ViCenQmV2ds.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: The Rituals, Episode 16
ViCenQmV2ds.one_line: Reciting the Quran in the standing of salah as a dignified act of love: vary your surahs, learn the last four juz, and stay present.
ViCenQmV2ds.summary: He explains why Quran is recited only while standing in salah: the servant stands upright with dignity to recite the King's words back to Him, while bowing and prostration are reserved for humility. The standing is an opportunity to show love and commitment, and the longer one recites, the more comfortably one can ask in sujud; the Prophet's night prayers were so long that Ibn Mas'ud once almost left. Since Allah's speech is the most intimate thing we have of Him, a relationship in which we do not love reciting it is already damaged; this is why the community preserves even the exact sound of each letter. Practically, he asks people to review what they know, feel the push to learn more, and aim to memorize the last four juz, which summarize the Quran. In each prayer, carry one theme from al-Fatihah to reflect on and choose a surah other than the one that rolls off the tongue. Praying in congregation lifts this burden because the imam carries it, but people who do not enjoy prayer pressure imams to rush. He asks the audience to add these adjustments gradually to the earlier tips on wudu and pausing before prayer.

outline.heading: Recitation belongs to the dignified standing
outline.gist: Quran is not recited in ruku or sujud; you stand with your head high to recite the King's words, and keep your face on the ground for humility alone.

outline.heading: Review and rotate the surahs you know
outline.gist: Look at what you have memorized and work to increase it; even two verses continuing from where you left off keep you engaged and present.

outline.heading: Long standing before long asking
outline.gist: The Prophet's long recitation built up to his requests; a five-second recitation followed by ten minutes of dua is out of balance.

outline.heading: Ibn Mas'ud behind the Prophet at night
outline.gist: Ibn Mas'ud nearly left during a prayer of several long surahs recited slowly and clearly, a sign of the Prophet's joy in reciting to Allah.

outline.heading: His word is what we have of Allah
outline.gist: We cannot see or hear Allah, but we have His speech; not loving to recite it means the relationship is already damaged, which is why children are taught Quran early.

outline.heading: Precision in recitation as an expression of love
outline.gist: The ummah preserved the book down to the sound of each letter, and drilling a reciter on one letter is respect, not excess.

outline.heading: Memorize the last four juz
outline.gist: Average Muslims should hold a portion of the Quran; the last four juz summarize its message and can be learned in four or five years.

outline.heading: This week's adjustment: one theme and a fresh surah
outline.gist: Alongside mindful wudu and the pause before prayer, reflect on one theme from al-Fatihah and avoid the default surah, to build concentration gradually.

outline.heading: Congregation lifts the burden
outline.gist: Behind an imam you can simply listen and reflect, since he carries the length and choice of recitation.

outline.heading: Impatience with imams
outline.gist: When he first led prayer here people complained about seconds of difference, and old men in a Syrian village shouted at a scholar for a long recitation; without understanding, prayer becomes unbearable.

outline.heading: Outro
